n0001.title: Cargo Cult Science
n0001.gist: Science works only when researchers practice strict honesty about their own errors, not merely copy its outward form.
n0001.question: Cargo Cult Science — why do studies that look scientific still fail to deliver real results? (a lecture)

n0006.title: Investigating pseudoscience
n0006.gist: Feynman surveys mysticism, ESP, and failed social sciences like education and criminal justice, arguing none of them actually work despite being treated as science.
n0006.question: Pseudoscience and failed fields — how can you tell a belief or method is scientifically empty? (several examples)

n0007.title: Framing the talk
n0007.gist: Introduces the talk's aim: showing how to avoid fooling yourself in science.

n0009.title: How science began
n0009.gist: Science arose when people began testing ideas against reality and discarding the ones that failed to work, unlike earlier superstitions.

n0011.title: A non-scientific world
n0011.gist: Despite the scientific age, many people still believe in UFOs, astrology, ESP, and similar unproven ideas, prompting an investigation into mysticism and altered states.

n0014.title: Massage anecdote
n0014.gist: A humorous episode in a hot tub shows people confidently naming body parts and practices with no real anatomical or scientific basis.

n0016.title: Uri Geller test
n0016.gist: A personal test of a famous psychic's claimed key-bending and mind-reading powers produced no results at all under direct observation.

n0018.title: Education and crime as pseudoscience
n0018.gist: Reading-education methods and criminal-rehabilitation programs are treated as scientific, yet decades of use have produced no measurable improvement.

n0022.title: Cocktail party test
n0022.gist: A joking rule of thumb — if a topic can be freely discussed at a party without embarrassment — marks subjects, like psychotherapy, where nobody truly knows the answers.

n0025.title: Cargo Cult Science
n0025.gist: Like islanders who rebuild runways and huts hoping planes will land again, some researchers copy science's outward form while missing the honesty that makes it work.
n0025.question: Cargo Cult Science — what exactly is missing when imitation science fails to deliver real results? (an analogy)

n0026.title: Cargo Cult Science
n0026.gist: The term describes research that mimics every outward step of scientific method yet consistently fails to produce real findings, like islanders imitating airstrips without planes ever landing.

n0028.title: Scientific integrity defined
n0028.gist: True scientific integrity means reporting every flaw, alternative explanation, and disagreeing fact about your own work, not just the evidence supporting your conclusion.

n0031.title: Giving all the information
n0031.gist: Researchers must present all relevant information, including what might undercut their own argument, so others can judge the work fairly rather than being steered toward one conclusion.

n0033.title: Advertising contrast
n0033.gist: A true but misleading ad claim about Wesson Oil shows that scientific integrity requires avoiding false implications, not merely avoiding outright lies, since reputations depend on careful honesty.

n0036.title: Difficulty is not the only problem
n0036.gist: Though these subjects are genuinely hard to study scientifically, that difficulty alone does not explain every failure — something else is still missing.

n0038.title: Self-deception and honesty
n0038.gist: Feynman shows through history and example that the deepest danger in science is fooling yourself, and that honesty toward laymen and funders is equally essential.
n0038.question: Scientific honesty — why must scientists guard most carefully against fooling themselves rather than others? (several examples)

n0039.title: Millikan's electron charge
n0039.gist: Successive measurements of the electron's charge crept slowly toward the correct value instead of jumping there at once, because scientists unconsciously distrusted results too different from Millikan's.

n0042.title: Not fooling yourself
n0042.gist: The first and hardest rule of scientific integrity is not to fool yourself, since you are the easiest person for your own biases to deceive.

n0045.title: Not fooling laymen
n0045.gist: Scientists owe the public the same honesty they owe each other, as shown by a colleague willing to overstate the usefulness of his research to keep funding flowing.

n0048.title: Publishing all results
n0048.gist: Honest science requires publishing results regardless of how they turn out, since selectively reporting only favorable outcomes, as advertisers do, distorts the truth.

n0050.title: Scientific advice to government
n0050.gist: Giving politicians scientific advice only when it favors their preferred outcome, while suppressing contrary findings, is not real scientific advice at all.

n0052.title: Case studies in good and bad science
n0052.gist: Contrasting psychology and physics examples show how skipping controls, reusing old data, or demanding fixed results corrupts experiments, while painstaking replication reveals real causes.
n0052.question: Good versus bad experiments — what separates careful science from Cargo Cult imitations? (five case studies)

n0053.title: Rat experiment proposal
n0053.gist: A student's plan to test rats under new conditions without first confirming she could replicate the original result shows a common, flawed shortcut in psychology research.

n0057.title: Physics example at NAL
n0057.gist: Pressure for quick new results at a major accelerator led a researcher to compare his data against an outdated experiment on different apparatus instead of repeating it properly.

n0059.title: Young's rat-running experiment
n0059.gist: By systematically eliminating every possible sensory clue — sight, smell, sound, texture — one researcher finally proved which cues rats truly used to find food.

n0064.title: Ignoring Young's findings
n0064.gist: Despite revealing the true conditions needed for valid rat experiments, later researchers ignored this careful work and kept running flawed experiments the old way.

n0066.title: ESP experiments critique
n0066.gist: Parapsychology experiments shrink their effects under scrutiny until they vanish, yet some researchers abandon the requirement of repeatable results and train only students who produce the desired outcome.

n0069.title: Closing wish
n0069.gist: Feynman closes by wishing graduates the freedom to keep scientific integrity even under institutional or financial pressure.
